measured_against: school pay (wages and salaries, state and local government, elementary and secondary schools)
why: Salaries are almost all of this category, and this is the published index of pay for the workers it covers: public elementary and secondary school employees. National, not Lunenburg; it tracks pay for the same jobs, so steps, experience and staffing mix are not in it.

measured_against: what benefits cost public employers (benefits, state and local government, all workers)
why: BLS publishes no benefits index for schools alone (series CIU3036110000000I does not exist); this is the nearest. It mixes health insurance with pensions. Retirement contributions are set by actuarial schedules, not by prices. The federal health insurance survey (AHRQ MEPS-IC) publishes state-level premiums for PRIVATE employers only, and state and local government premiums nationally or by region, so it was not used.

measured_against: grocery prices, Boston area (food at home)
why: Lunenburg runs its own food service: in the school MUNIS journal, FY2023 to FY2026, the largest payees on its supplies line are food distributors, and its other large lines are staff pay. Food at home prices what is bought; food away from home would price restaurant labour and margins. The staff-pay part is not priced separately here; the page’s table prints both indexes, so a reader can see how far apart they are.

measured_against: school pay (wages and salaries, state and local government, elementary and secondary schools)
why: Custodial services are school employees’ pay. Weighted by DESE’s own FY2009 spending on this code.

Heating and utilities are energy bills. The Boston-area household energy series (CUURS11ASAH21) stops at December 2024, so it cannot reach FY2025; the Northeast series is the nearest that does. Household rates, not a school’s contract rates. Weighted by DESE’s FY2009 spending on these codes.

why: No published price index for school building maintenance that this project found; household prices stand in. Weighted by DESE’s FY2009 spending on these codes.

fiscal_year_average: Jul, Sep, Nov, Jan, Mar, May
why: The state’s Operational Services Division sets approved special education school prices by an inflation factor each year, but mass.gov publishes only the current estimate: on 20 October 2026 it served the FY2026 workbook (FY26-Estimated-Inflation-Rates-25Feb2026_0.xlsx) and the FY2027 memo (CIFFY27_memo100125.pdf), and answered 404 for every earlier fiscal year asked, FY2009 to FY2025. The annual factor is also not the whole price: a school can be granted extraordinary relief. No year-by-year series could be built from published documents.
